Cell injury

  • Cell injury occurs when stress exceeds cell’s ability to adapt
  • Likelihood of injury depends on
  • Type of stress
  • Severity of stress
  • Type of cell affected

Causes of cell injury

  • Hypoxia
  • Infection
  • Toxins
  • Immunologic reactions
  • Genetic mutations
  • Nutritional imbalances
  • Physical agents

Different injurious stimuli

  • Result in a similar sequence of alterations in most cell types

Hypoxia

  • Low oxygen delivery to tissues
  • Hypoxia impairs oxidative phosphorylation
  • Results in decreased ATP

Causes of hypoxia

  • Ischemia
  • Hypoxemia
  • Decreased O2 carrying capacity of the blood

Ischemia

  • Decreased blood flow through an organ

Hypoxemia

  • low partial pressure of O2 in blood (PaO2 < 60 mmHg , SaO2 < 90%)

Decrease O2 carrying capacity

  • Arises with Hb loss or dysfunction
  • Examples: Anemia and CO poisoning and Methemoglobinemia

Anemia

  • Decrease in RBC mass
  • PaO2 normal , SaO2 normal

CO poisoning

  • CO binds Hb Stronger than O2
  • PaO2 normal, SaO2 decreased
  • exposures include smoke from fires and exhaust from cars or gas heaters

Clinical features

  • Classic finding is cherry red appearance of skin
  • Early sign of exposure is headache
  • Significant exposure can lead to coma and death

Methemoglobinemia

  • Iron in heme is oxidized to Fe+3 , which cannot bind O2
  • PaO2 is normal , SaO2 is decreased
  • seen with oxidant stress (e.g. sulfa and nitrate drugs) or in newborns

Clinical Features and Treatment

  • Classic finding is cyanosis with chocolate colored blood
  • treatment is IV methylene blue which helps reduce Fe3+ back to Fe 2+ state

Low ATP

  • Low ATP disrupts key cellular functions
  • Na+ - k+ pump
  • Ca2+ pump
  • Aerobic glycolysis

Initial phase of injury is reversible

  • Hallmark is cellular swelling
  • Leads to loss of
  • Microvilli
  • Membrane blebbing
  • Swelling of RER

Other features of reversible cell injury

  • Fatty changes
  • Mitochondrial changes include swelling , appearance of phospholipid rich amorphous densities
  • Nuclear alterations:
  • clumping of chromatin
  • Appearance of myelin figures

Cell death

  • Persistent or excessive injury => irreversible injury (cell death)
  • Hallmark is membrane damage
  • Will be the topic of the next video
